newsitem.title: USA: U.S. economic growth slowed in third quarter.
newsitem.headline: U.S. economic growth slowed in third quarter.

text.p: The economy's third-quarter slowdown was slightly less abrupt than previously thought, the Commerce Department said on Friday, mainly because production for inventory was stronger than estimated a month ago.

The nation's gross domestic product expanded at a 2.1 percent annual rate in the three months from July through September. That was still less than half the 4.7 percent pace posted during the second quarter but fractionally higher than the 2 percent rate estimated a month ago, the department said in its second and final look at third-quarter performance.

Wall Street economists had forecast third-quarter GDP growth would be revised down to 1.8 percent instead of up. But the revision was minimal and did not alter the picture of a cooling economy at mid-summer after a sizzling first half.

"It came in fairly close to forecasts and it is for the third quarter," said Hugh Johnson, chief investment officer at First Albany Corp. "The focus in the market now is on the fourth quarter and beyond."

"Growth was markedly lower in the third quarter than in the second, and most components contributed to the slowdown except business investment in structures, equipment and inventories," the Commerce Department said.

The department originally estimated GDP grew at a 2.2 percent annual rate in the third quarter. But it revised it down to 2 percent a month ago and finally back up to 2.1 percent in this final look, based on updated economic information.
Early indications are that the fourth quarter will see continued moderate growth around a so-called "trend rate" of 2.25 percent a year.
No official estimate of fourth-quarter economic growth will be available until a month from now.

Reports on fourth-quarter activity so far are mixed, ranging from a pickup in homebuilding last month, which would bolster growth, to more applications for weekly jobless claims last week, which suggests a moderating job market.
GDP measures the value of all goods and services produced by workers and capital within U.S. borders.

Consumer spending is expected to strengthen in the current quarter after weakening sharply in the third quarter. Spending advanced at a revised 0.5 percent annual rate in the third quarter, down from last month's estimated 0.6 percent rise and barely a fraction of the second quarter's strong 3.4 percent rate of advance.
Reports indicate that spending in the key shopping season that started after Thanksgiving and runs up to Christmas is at least moderately stronger than last year.

But there is little to indicate the economy is poised for anything more than continued modest growth. Earlier this week, the Federal Reserve opted to keep interest rates steady at a final policy-setting session of the year.

After cutting rates by a quarter percentage point in January, the Fed has held policy steady as economic growth has first waxed and then waned, showing few signs of generating strong inflationary pressures.
Two inflation measures in the GDP report showed controlled price rises with only a scant revision upward in each.

The implicit price deflator advanced at a revised 1.7 percent annual rate in the third quarter instead of the 1.6 percent reported previously, compared with 1.8 percent in the second quarter. The fixed-weights measure of price changes rose 2 percent instead of 1.9 percent compared with 2.2 percent in the second quarter.
A report from the private Conference Board in New York on Thursday cautioned that rising global demand for food and energy contained the seeds of a potential speed-up in inflation.
"Food and energy prices are currently rising faster than the core inflation rate -- a red flag for future inflation," the Conference Board said.

During the third quarter, businesses increased inventories by $34.5 billion instead of $32.8 billion, the governemnt estimated. That was nearly five times the $7.1 billion worth of goods they put into inventories in the second quarter and added powerfully to the overall third-quarter GDP advance.
The department also revised down slightly its estimate of imports in the third quarter, which means international trade was slightly less of a drag on economic growth during the summer.

Business investment was revised up slightly to show companies boosted spending to a $30.9 billion annual rate in the third quarter instead of at a $29.9-billion pace. That was quadruple the $7-billion annual rate of increase in business investment posted during the second quarter.
